title: Petra and the Tide
premise: Emrys Galloway, a lighthouse keeper's grandson and part-time novelist, has spent twelve years hiding in the tidal village of Porthmara after a family scandal he believes was his fault. When a letter postmarked eleven years ago surfaces—written by his dying grandfather and lost in a wall cavity—it reveals that the inheritance, the fire, and the betrayal were not what Emrys remembered, and that his childhood love, Petra Voss, never abandoned him at all. As developers close in on the lighthouse and Petra returns to broker the sale, Emrys must finally speak the confession he has rehearsed for a decade before the truth is buried forever under concrete and tide. In the end, he chooses truth over safety: the lighthouse is saved through Petra's testimony, his novel is published under his real name, and the two of them stand together on the headland as the light comes on.
about_author: Quentin Joubert is the pen name of a former coastal surveyor who spent nine years mapping erosion along the Cornish and Breton shores before turning to fiction. He writes in the off-season from a converted net loft, where the sound of the water dictates his sentence lengths.

chapters.title: The Weight of Small Steps
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. A quiet portrait of his carefully rationed life in Porthmara: mornings at the chandlery, evenings drafting a novel he never submits, rituals that keep memory at bay. The beat is deceptive calm—the reader senses the walls are load-bearing and brittle.

chapters.title: What the Wall Kept
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Renovation tremors crack open a cavity in the old keeper's cottage, revealing a sealed envelope postmarked eleven years ago in his grandfather's hand. He cannot bring himself to open it. The beat is dread wrapped in curiosity.

chapters.title: Petra, Arriving
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. She steps off the ferry with a developer's contract and a face Emrys hasn't seen in twelve years. She is composed, professional, and lying about why she came back. The beat is a collision disguised as small talk.

chapters.title: The Sentence Rehearsed
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Flashback to the night of the fire twelve years ago—what Emrys said, what he failed to say, and how he fled. We learn the sentence he has rehearsed a decade: 'It was my fault, and you were right to leave.' The beat is guilt calcified into identity.

chapters.title: Terms of Sale
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. In the village hall, she presents the development plan for the headland; the lighthouse itself is excluded only by an easement her firm intends to contest. Emrys speaks against it publicly—the first time he's raised his voice in years. The beat is reluctant courage.

chapters.title: Grandfather's Ink
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Alone at last, he opens the letter. His grandfather writes that he knew who truly started the fire—and it was not Emrys—and that he left the cottage to both grandchildren jointly. The beat is vertigo: the foundation of twelve years of self-punishment cracks.

chapters.title: Half an Inheritance
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Her firm informs her the joint deed complicates the acquisition; she must get Emrys to sign. She requests a meeting knowing it will be personal. The beat is divided loyalty—her career, her conscience, and the boy she never stopped loving.

chapters.title: Low Tide Confessions
chapters.summary: Dual POV alternating scenes. Trapped together by the tide in the causeway cave where they played as children, they circle old wounds without naming them. Emrys almost says the sentence; Petra almost tells him what she saw that night. The beat is intimacy sharpened by withheld truths.

chapters.title: The Firm's Patience
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Her director arrives unannounced, pressuring her to use Emrys's fragile reputation as leverage—rumors about the fire still circulate. She stalls, and realizes her employer knows more about that night than she does. The beat is rising institutional menace.

chapters.title: A Novel Nobody Reads
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. A young editor who found his manuscript online contacts him; the book is transparently about the fire and Petra. Terrified of exposure, he nearly declines. Instead he asks her to hold it 'until I'm ready.' The beat is hope requiring bravery he doesn't yet have.

chapters.title: What Petra Saw
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Flashback eleven years: the true origin of the fire—Emrys's uncle, drunk, knocking over a lamp during an argument over the inheritance—and Petra's silence, bought by her father's fear of the Galloway name. The beat is tragic symmetry: both believed their silence protected the other.

chapters.title: Storm Warning
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. A winter storm damages the lighthouse lamp room; the council declares it beyond economic repair, strengthening the developer's case. Emrys organizes villagers to tarp the roof overnight. The beat is community as antidote to isolation.

chapters.title: Signatures
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Petra presents the buyout papers; Emrys refuses, revealing the joint deed and the letter's existence. Petra realizes her firm may have suppressed knowledge of the second heir all along. The beat is alliance forming across enemy lines.

chapters.title: The Director's File
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Searching the firm's archives, she finds a surveyor's report from eleven years ago noting the fire's cause—an uncle's negligence—filed and buried to secure the original Galloway land option. The beat is cold fury and a choice taking shape.

chapters.title: Rehearsal Interrupted
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Emrys finally attempts the rehearsed sentence with Petra—but she stops him: 'You've been confessing to the wrong crime for twelve years.' She can't yet say what she knows. The beat is devastating near-miss, tension at fever pitch.

chapters.title: Betrayal or Loyalty
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Her director threatens to fire her and bury the report permanently unless she delivers Emrys's signature within the week. She photographs the file instead. The beat is the theme made flesh: loyalty to people versus loyalty to power.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Dual POV. At the council hearing on the easement, the firm springs its case—and produces the old rumor of Emrys's guilt as character evidence. Publicly humiliated, Emrys freezes. The beat is the darkest hour; the rehearsed sentence dies in his throat.

chapters.title: Light On
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. That night, Emrys climbs the tower and hand-lights the derelict lamp—a beacon visible to the whole village—as word spreads of the hearing. Villagers gather below. The beat is defiance; the invisible man makes himself unmistakable.

chapters.title: The Truth, Spoken
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Petra takes the stand uninvited, presents the buried surveyor's report, and testifies to what she witnessed eleven years ago—clearing Emrys and implicating her own father's cover-up. The beat is cathartic climax: truth chosen over every safe lie.

chapters.title: Aftermath of Air
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. In the emptied hearing room, Emrys finally says the sentence—not the rehearsed one, but a new one: 'I stayed away because I thought I deserved to be alone.' Petra answers with her own confession of silence. The beat is grief and relief entwined.

chapters.title: Easement Granted
chapters.summary: Dual POV. The council upholds the easement; the firm withdraws, its director resigning amid inquiry. The village begins restoring the lighthouse; Emrys signs nothing except a publishing contract under his real name. The beat is earned restoration, power checked by truth.

chapters.title: Petra and the Tide
chapters.summary: Dual POV closing scene. One year later: the relit lighthouse, the published novel titled after this very night, and the two of them on the headland at spring tide, no longer keeping count of small safe steps. The final line lands on the light sweeping out to sea. The beat is quiet, hard-won joy.
